Line up a row of Navy fighters and they all look more or less the same, grey on grey, built to disappear against the sky. So for decades, one aircraft stopped everybody who walked past it: a single F-14 Tomcat painted glossy black from nose to tail, with a white Playboy bunny sitting right on the fin. It had a name, "Vandy 1," and most people just called it the Black Bunny.

The jet belonged to VX-4, "The Evaluators," the Navy's Air Test and Evaluation Squadron based at Point Mugu, California. These were the people who wrung out new missiles, radars, and systems before the fleet ever saw them. By long tradition, the squadron commander's personal aircraft flew under the call sign "Vandy 1," short for "Vanderbilt 1," and it was always the black one, painted that way on purpose so there was no mistaking whose jet it was.

The bunny came first, and it came with a story. Navy squadrons had been putting rabbits on their tails since the 1950s, but VX-4 made it famous. The black bunny scheme started back in 1969 on an F-4 Phantom used for night testing. Then in 1971, Playboy's lawyers noticed, and the company warned the Navy it might take legal action over the logo. Instead of a fight, they struck a deal: Playboy backed off and actually supplied the squadron an official bunny stencil, so the Navy could keep painting it the right way. No lawsuit, just a handshake and a stencil.

The bunny moved onto the Tomcat in 1985, when two F-14As were assigned to the squadron and given the black treatment. By 1990 the Black Bunnies were flying F-14As in permanent gloss black, and the jet became a genuine flight-line celebrity, the one everybody wanted a photo of, the one that looked like it had wandered in from a movie set.

It couldn't last. In 1994, VX-4 merged with another test squadron to form VX-9, and the bunny quietly disappeared from the Tomcats. But the Navy gave it one last ride: the very last F-14 ever built was painted up as the Black Bunny for its farewell flights before being parked as a gate guardian. Today the livery is gone, but the legend isn't. In an age of grey airplanes designed to be invisible, somebody once flew a jet-black Tomcat with a bunny on the tail, and dared you not to look.

NATO is being tested along its southeastern edge, and this week the alliance is meeting to decide what to do about it. Over the weekend, Romanian F-16 fighter jets intercepted and downed two drones that had crossed into the country's airspace from the Black Sea.

What stands out is how routine this is becoming. Romania says it has recorded 35 unauthorized drone incursions so far in 2026, compared with 9 in all of 2025, and has downed six of them this year after downing none the year before. The defense ministry identified the latest two as Geran-type attack drones flying at around 280 mph, a design associated with Russia's arsenal, though officials have not formally blamed Russia for this specific incident.

The response is moving up to the alliance level. NATO's governing body, the North Atlantic Council, is set to meet in Brussels, and Romania's foreign minister said the talks will focus on expanding NATO's presence in the Black Sea region and increasing surveillance. Bulgaria, which shares the same coastline, has asked allies for additional aircraft and counter-drone equipment.

The incursions come as the war in neighboring Ukraine continues to brush up against NATO's borders. The alliance's secretary general, Mark Rutte, met Romanian and Bulgarian leaders the week before and said NATO had strengthened its posture along its eastern flank.

None of this points to a wider war. Most of these drones appear to be strays or probes rather than deliberate strikes on NATO itself. But the numbers are climbing fast, and the alliance is being forced to work out, in real time, how to defend a long stretch of coastline against cheap drones without overreacting to every one that wanders across the line. That problem isn't going away.
